{"questions": [
{"id": "p1", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (divisibility via reduction modulo a linear expression)", "error_type": "omitted_case", "question": "Find the sum of the positive integers n such that 2n − 1 divides n^2 + 26.", "answer": 100, "target_wrong": 89, "error_description": "The divisor 21 of 105 is left out of the list 1, 3, 5, 7, 15, 35, 105, so the solution n = 11 (where 2n−1 = 21 divides 121+26 = 147) is missing.", "cases": ["2n-1=1 -> n=1", "2n-1=3 -> n=2", "2n-1=5 -> n=3", "2n-1=7 -> n=4", "2n-1=15 -> n=8", "2n-1=21 -> n=11", "2n-1=35 -> n=18", "2n-1=105 -> n=53"], "solution": "Since 2n−1 is odd, gcd(2n−1, 4) = 1, so 2n−1 | n^2+26 iff 2n−1 | 4(n^2+26) = 4n^2+104. Now 4n^2 + 104 = (2n−1)(2n+1) + 105, so the condition is 2n−1 | 105 = 3·5·7. The divisors of 105 are 1, 3, 5, 7, 15, 21, 35, 105, giving n = (d+1)/2 = 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 11, 18, 53. Each works (e.g. n = 11: 147 = 7·21; n = 53: 2835 = 27·105). The sum is 1+2+3+4+8+11+18+53 = 100.", "check_code": "print(sum(n for n in range(1,100000) if (n*n+26)%(2*n-1)==0))"},
{"id": "p2", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (difference of squares, parity of factor pairs)", "error_type": "omitted_case", "question": "Find the sum of the positive integers n for which n^2 + 72n is a perfect square.", "answer": 577, "target_wrong": 528, "error_description": "The factor pair 4·81 = 324 is skipped when listing the factor pairs of 324 (the list jumps from 3·108 to 6·54), so the solution n = 4+81−36 = 49 is omitted.", "cases": ["(1,324) -> n=289", "(2,162) -> n=128", "(3,108) -> n=75", "(4,81) -> n=49", "(6,54) -> n=24", "(9,36) -> n=9", "(12,27) -> n=3"], "solution": "Write n^2 + 72n = m^2 with m ≥ 0. Completing the square, (n+36)^2 − m^2 = 1296, i.e. (n+36−m)(n+36+m) = 1296. Both factors have the same parity and their product is even, so both are even: write them as 2d and 2e with de = 324, d ≤ e. If d = e then m = 0 and n(n+72) = 0, impossible for positive n, so d < e. Then n + 36 = d + e. The factor pairs of 324 = 2^2·3^4 with d < e are (1,324), (2,162), (3,108), (4,81), (6,54), (9,36), (12,27), giving n = 289, 128, 75, 49, 24, 9, 3. (Check: 49·121 = 77^2, 3·75 = 15^2, etc.) The sum is 289+128+75+49+24+9+3 = 577.", "check_code": "import math\ns=0\nfor n in range(1,100000):\n    v=n*n+72*n\n    r=math.isqrt(v)\n    if r*r==v:\n        s+=n\nprint(s)"},
{"id": "p3", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (cycles of powers mod 10)", "error_type": "omitted_case", "question": "Find the sum of the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which n^n and n have the same units digit.", "answer": 3110, "target_wrong": 2570, "error_description": "The units digit 9 is grouped with the failing digit 4 (both have period 2) and discarded, but 9^n ends in 9 for every odd n and every n ending in 9 is odd; the ten numbers 9, 19, ..., 99 (sum 540) are omitted.", "cases": ["units digit 0: 10,20,...,100 (sum 550)", "units digit 1: 1,11,...,91 (sum 460)", "units digit 5: 5,...,95 (sum 500)", "units digit 6: 6,...,96 (sum 510)", "units digit 9: 9,...,99 (sum 540)", "units digit 3 with n ≡ 1 mod 4: 13,33,53,73,93 (sum 265)", "units digit 7 with n ≡ 1 mod 4: 17,37,57,77,97 (sum 285)", "units digits 2,4,8: never (n even forces 2^n,4^n,8^n to end in 4 or 6)"], "solution": "Work by the units digit d of n. If d ∈ {0,1,5,6} then every power of n ends in d, so all ten such n ≤ 100 work: sums 550, 460, 500, 510. If d = 9, then 9^n ends in 9 iff n is odd, and every n ending in 9 is odd, so 9, 19, ..., 99 all work: sum 540. If d = 4, 4^n ends in 4 iff n is odd, but n ending in 4 is even, so none work; similarly for d = 2 and d = 8 (2^n and 8^n end in 2 or 8 only for odd n). If d = 3, 3^n ends in 3 iff n ≡ 1 (mod 4); among 3, 13, ..., 93 this holds for 13, 33, 53, 73, 93 (sum 265). If d = 7, 7^n ends in 7 iff n ≡ 1 (mod 4), giving 17, 37, 57, 77, 97 (sum 285). Total: 550+460+500+510+540+265+285 = 3110.", "check_code": "print(sum(n for n in range(1,101) if pow(n,n,10)==n%10))"},
{"id": "p4", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (products divisible by a modulus, gcd casework)", "error_type": "omitted_case", "question": "How many ordered pairs (a, b) of integers with 1 ≤ a ≤ 36 and 1 ≤ b ≤ 36 satisfy ab ≡ 0 (mod 36)?", "answer": 168, "target_wrong": 150, "error_description": "The divisor 18 of 36 is dropped from the list of possible values of gcd(a,36), so the case a = 18 (where b may be any of the 18 even numbers) is omitted.", "cases": ["gcd(a,36)=1: 12 values of a, 1 b each (12)", "gcd=2: 6 values of a, 2 b each (12)", "gcd=3: 4 values of a, 3 b each (12)", "gcd=4: 6 values of a, 4 b each (24)", "gcd=6: 2 values of a, 6 b each (12)", "gcd=9: 2 values of a, 9 b each (18)", "gcd=12: 2 values of a, 12 b each (24)", "gcd=18: a=18, 18 values of b (18)", "gcd=36: a=36, 36 values of b (36)"], "solution": "Fix a and let g = gcd(a, 36). Then 36 | ab iff (36/g) | b, and there are exactly g multiples of 36/g in 1..36. The number of a in 1..36 with gcd(a,36) = g is φ(36/g). So the count is Σ_{g | 36} g·φ(36/g): g=1: 1·12 = 12; g=2: 2·6 = 12; g=3: 3·4 = 12; g=4: 4·6 = 24; g=6: 6·2 = 12; g=9: 9·2 = 18; g=12: 12·2 = 24; g=18: 18·1 = 18; g=36: 36·1 = 36. Total 12+12+12+24+12+18+24+18+36 = 168.", "check_code": "print(sum(1 for a in range(1,37) for b in range(1,37) if (a*b)%36==0))"},
{"id": "p5", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (divisibility by 9 via digit sums)", "error_type": "omitted_case", "question": "Find the sum of the positive integers N < 1000 such that N is divisible by 9 and every digit of N is odd.", "answer": 4437, "target_wrong": 4104, "error_description": "When listing triples of odd digits with sum 9, the repeated-digit triple 3+3+3 is missed (only 1+1+7 and 1+3+5 are found), so N = 333 is omitted.", "cases": ["one-digit: 9", "two-digit, digit sum 18: 99", "three-digit, digit sum 27: 999", "three-digit, digits {1,1,7}: 117, 171, 711 (sum 999)", "three-digit, digits {1,3,5}: six permutations (sum 1998)", "three-digit, digits {3,3,3}: 333"], "solution": "N is divisible by 9 iff its digit sum is a multiple of 9. One-digit: only 9. Two-digit: two odd digits have even sum between 2 and 18, so the sum must be 18, giving 99. Three-digit: the sum of three odd digits is odd and at most 27, so it is 9 or 27. Sum 27 gives 999. Sum 9 with digits from {1,3,5,7,9}: the multisets are {1,1,7}, {1,3,5}, {3,3,3}. These give 117, 171, 711 (sum 999); the six permutations of 1,3,5, whose sum is 2·(1+3+5)·111 = 1998; and 333. Total: 9 + 99 + 999 + 999 + 1998 + 333 = 4437.", "check_code": "print(sum(N for N in range(1,1000) if N%9==0 and all(int(d)%2==1 for d in str(N))))"},
{"id": "p6", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (idempotents mod 60 via CRT)", "error_type": "omitted_case", "question": "Find the sum of the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which n^2 − n is divisible by 60.", "answer": 743, "target_wrong": 683, "error_description": "The residue class n ≡ 0 (mod 60) is omitted: the solver lists the classes 1, 16, 21, 25, 36, 40, 45 from the CRT choices but forgets the all-zero choice, dropping n = 60.", "cases": ["n ≡ 0 mod 60: 60", "n ≡ 1 mod 60: 1, 61", "n ≡ 16 mod 60: 16, 76", "n ≡ 21 mod 60: 21, 81", "n ≡ 25 mod 60: 25, 85", "n ≡ 36 mod 60: 36, 96", "n ≡ 40 mod 60: 40, 100", "n ≡ 45 mod 60: 45"], "solution": "We need 60 | n(n−1). Since n and n−1 are coprime, 4 | n(n−1) iff n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4); similarly n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 3) and n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 5). By CRT there are 2^3 = 8 residue classes mod 60: 0, 1, 16, 21, 25, 36, 40, 45. In 1..100 these give 60; 1, 61; 16, 76; 21, 81; 25, 85; 36, 96; 40, 100; 45. The sum is 60 + 62 + 92 + 102 + 110 + 132 + 140 + 45 = 743.", "check_code": "print(sum(n for n in range(1,101) if (n*n-n)%60==0))"},
{"id": "p7", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (binomial expansion mod 1000)", "error_type": "algebra_slip", "question": "Find the remainder when 11^2024 + 9^2024 is divided by 1000.", "answer": 202, "target_wrong": 682, "error_description": "In expanding 9^2024 = (10 − 1)^2024, the linear term is taken as +2024·10 instead of −2024·10 (the sign of (−1)^2023 is dropped), giving 841 instead of 361 for 9^2024 mod 1000 and a final answer of 682.", "cases": [], "solution": "Expand with the binomial theorem; terms with 10^3 or higher vanish mod 1000. 11^2024 = (1+10)^2024 ≡ 1 + 2024·10 + C(2024,2)·100 (mod 1000). C(2024,2) = 2024·2023/2 = 2047276, so C(2024,2)·100 ≡ 600, and 2024·10 ≡ 240. Hence 11^2024 ≡ 1 + 240 + 600 = 841. Similarly 9^2024 = (−1+10)^2024 ≡ 1 − 2024·10 + C(2024,2)·100 ≡ 1 − 240 + 600 = 361 (mod 1000). (Check via CRT: 9^2024 ≡ 1 mod 8 and 9^24 ≡ 111 mod 125, consistent with 361.) The sum is 841 + 361 = 1202 ≡ 202 (mod 1000).", "check_code": "print((pow(11,2024,1000)+pow(9,2024,1000))%1000)"},
{"id": "p8", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (remainder conditions, inclusion-exclusion)", "error_type": "misread_condition", "question": "How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000 leave a remainder of 1 when divided by exactly one of the three numbers 3, 5, and 7?", "answer": 419, "target_wrong": 543, "error_description": "The condition 'exactly one of 3, 5, 7' is read as 'at least one of 3, 5, 7', so the solver computes |A ∪ B ∪ C| = 677 − 144 + 10 = 543 instead of the exactly-one count.", "cases": [], "solution": "Let A, B, C be the sets of n in 1..1000 with n ≡ 1 mod 3, mod 5, mod 7 respectively. |A| = 334 (n = 3k+1, k = 0..333), |B| = 200, |C| = 143. Intersections correspond to n ≡ 1 modulo 15, 21, 35, 105: |A∩B| = 67, |A∩C| = 48, |B∩C| = 29, |A∩B∩C| = 10. The number of n lying in exactly one set is |A|+|B|+|C| − 2(|A∩B|+|A∩C|+|B∩C|) + 3|A∩B∩C| = 677 − 2·144 + 30 = 419.", "check_code": "print(sum(1 for n in range(1,1001) if sum(1 for m in (3,5,7) if n%m==1)==1))"},
{"id": "p9", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (solutions of n^2 ≡ −1, union of residue classes)", "error_type": "double_counting", "question": "How many positive integers n ≤ 1000 are there for which n^2 + 1 is divisible by 5 or by 13?", "answer": 492, "target_wrong": 554, "error_description": "The two counts 400 (divisible by 5) and 154 (divisible by 13) are added without subtracting the 62 values of n for which n^2 + 1 is divisible by 65, double counting the overlap.", "cases": [], "solution": "n^2 ≡ −1 (mod 5) iff n ≡ 2 or 3 (mod 5); each class has 200 members in 1..1000, so 400 values. n^2 ≡ −1 (mod 13) iff n ≡ 5 or 8 (mod 13); since 1000 = 13·76 + 12, each nonzero residue class has 77 members, so 154 values. Both hold iff n^2 ≡ −1 (mod 65), i.e. n ≡ 8, 18, 47, or 57 (mod 65) (e.g. 8^2+1 = 65, 18^2+1 = 325, 47^2+1 = 2210, 57^2+1 = 3250). Since 1000 = 65·15 + 25, residues 8 and 18 give 16 values each and residues 47 and 57 give 15 each: 62 in total. By inclusion-exclusion the answer is 400 + 154 − 62 = 492.", "check_code": "print(sum(1 for n in range(1,1001) if (n*n+1)%5==0 or (n*n+1)%13==0))"},
{"id": "p10", "topic": "number theory: modular arithmetic and residues (simultaneous congruences, counting terms in a progression)", "error_type": "off_by_one", "question": "Find the sum of the positive integers n < 500 that satisfy n ≡ 7 (mod 12) and n ≡ 4 (mod 9).", "answer": 3710, "target_wrong": 3211, "error_description": "The number of terms 31, 67, ..., 499 is taken as floor((500−31)/36) = 13 instead of 13 + 1 = 14, so the boundary term n = 499 is dropped and the sum becomes 13·(31+463)/2 = 3211.", "cases": [], "solution": "Both congruences force n ≡ 1 (mod 3), so they are compatible; lcm(12, 9) = 36. Write n = 4 + 9j; then 4 + 9j ≡ 7 (mod 12) gives 9j ≡ 3 (mod 12), i.e. 3j ≡ 1 (mod 4), so j ≡ 3 (mod 4) and n ≡ 4 + 27 = 31 (mod 36). The solutions below 500 are n = 31 + 36k with 31 + 36k ≤ 499, i.e. k = 0, 1, ..., 13: fourteen terms 31, 67, ..., 499. Their sum is 14·(31 + 499)/2 = 14·265 = 3710.", "check_code": "print(sum(n for n in range(1,500) if n%12==7 and n%9==4))"}
]}
